payload.task_text:
I am working on my PhD thesis and I need help putting together the literature review section for Chapter 2, which focuses on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In my workspace there is a compressed archive called research_notes.tar.gz that contains some preliminary notes I have been keeping in markdown files about background concepts, key research questions, and related retrieval methods. I would appreciate it if you could first extract that archive so we can see what is in there, and then read through the notes to understand the context of my research.

My research focus and the key concepts I am tracking are stored in a knowledge graph file located at memory/memory.json in the workspace. Please read that to understand the scope and direction of my literature review.

After familiarizing yourself with my notes and research focus, I need you to search academic databases for recent and foundational papers on Retrieval-Augmented Generation. I am looking for approximately five key papers that cover the topic from different angles, including the original RAG formulation, survey papers, self-reflective retrieval approaches, recursive retrieval methods, and practical system-building perspectives. For each paper you find, please download it and read through its content to understand the main contributions. I would also like you to look at the source manuscripts of these papers to examine the methodology sections in more detail, since the methodology comparison is an important part of my literature review.

Once you have gathered all of this information, please store the key findings in my knowledge graph so that I can reference them later. Then create a Word document called Literature_Review.docx in my workspace. The document should begin with an introduction section that provides an overview of Retrieval-Augmented Generation as a research area and explains why it matters for knowledge-intensive natural language processing tasks. Following the introduction, include a dedicated section for each of the five papers you found. Each paper section should clearly state the paper title, the authors, the publication year, a description of the main contribution, and a discussion of the methodology used. After covering all five papers, end the document with a conclusion section that synthesizes the key themes, identifies common patterns across the papers, and suggests directions for future research. Please make sure the writing flows naturally and reads like a proper academic literature review rather than a collection of disconnected summaries.

A few things to keep in mind while you work.

First, the databases may return papers that are not actually about Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including papers from other fields. Judge each result by its title and abstract. The review should cover only the papers that are genuinely about RAG; please do not include or discuss unrelated papers in Literature_Review.docx.

Second, the deliverable is a single file, Literature_Review.docx, and it must end up complete and well-formed. It must be created exactly once, by exactly one designated agent, and only after all of the paper content has been gathered. Any agent that is responsible for only a portion of this task (for example, researching a subset of the papers) must NOT create, write, overwrite, or append to Literature_Review.docx; that agent should instead return its findings in its report or write them to its own separately named intermediate file that no other agent writes to. Do not have several agents append to or rewrite the same document file, as that will corrupt or overwrite it. A safe way to work in parallel is to have each agent take responsibility for a distinct subset of the papers and return its findings, and then have one agent assemble the final document exactly once, after all of the findings are in.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, use exactly one research wave. The main agent must extract `research_notes.tar.gz` once without overwriting files, read the extracted Markdown and `memory/memory.json`, and freeze these five non-overlapping topics: original RAG formulation; RAG survey; self-reflective/adaptive retrieval; recursive/hierarchical retrieval; and practical system building.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 explore sub-agents in parallel:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): Explore 0 owns only the original RAG formulation topic.
   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): Explore 1 owns only the strongest RAG survey topic.
   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): Explore 2 owns only self-reflective or adaptive retrieval.
   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): Explore 3 owns only recursive or hierarchical retrieval.
   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): Explore 4 owns only practical RAG system building.

Each explore sub-agent searches only its assigned topic, rejects off-topic titles/abstracts, selects exactly one distinct paper, downloads and reads that paper, inspects the available LaTeX methodology sections, and writes one uniquely named compact evidence JSON containing topic, stable ID, exact title, authors, year, contribution, methodology, evidence section names, and limitations. Return only the JSON path, stable ID, and compact search/read controls. No sub-agent may modify the knowledge graph or create `Literature_Review.docx`.

After Wave 1, the main agent verifies five distinct IDs and five topic slots, then directly owns both remaining outputs. Update the existing knowledge graph by adding only the five source-supported paper entities and relationships while preserving unrelated nodes. Create `Literature_Review.docx` exactly once with one bulk structured write: title; Introduction; five sections in the frozen topic order, each stating the exact title, authors, year, main contribution, and methodology; and a synthetic Conclusion with common themes and future research. Use only the five retained papers, exclude all rejected results, read the graph and document back once, and finish without another sub-agent or verification wave.

You are a planning sub-agent. Decompose the following task into an ordered, executable plan. You have READ-ONLY tools (filesystem reads, arxiv_local read/list/search, arxiv-latex reads, scholarly search, memory read/search). Do NOT mutate anything — only produce a plan.

CONTEXT:
The main agent is helping a PhD student build the literature review for Chapter 2 of their thesis, focused on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The workspace is at:
/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace

Inside the workspace:
- research_notes.tar.gz — a compressed archive of the student's preliminary markdown notes (background concepts, key research questions, related retrieval methods).
- memory/memory.json — a knowledge graph file with the student's research focus and key concepts.
- The full task will use these tools: mcp__filesystem__* (read/write), mcp__terminal__run_command (extraction, inspection), mcp__arxiv_local__* (search/list/download/read papers), mcp__arxiv-latex__* (paper abstracts/sections/LaTeX source), mcp__scholarly__search-arxiv / search-google-scholar, mcp__memory__* (knowledge graph create/read/update), mcp__word__* (create and edit .docx).

THE FULL TASK (to be planned):
1. Extract research_notes.tar.gz into the workspace and read the markdown notes to understand background concepts, key research questions, and related retrieval methods.
2. Read memory/memory.json to understand the research scope/direction.
3. Search academic databases for ~5 key papers on RAG covering different angles: (a) the original RAG formulation, (b) a survey paper, (c) self-reflective retrieval approaches, (d) recursive retrieval methods, (e) practical system-building perspectives. Judge relevance by title and abstract — EXCLUDE papers not genuinely about RAG.
4. For each paper: download it (mcp__arxiv_local__download_paper), read its content (mcp__arxiv_local__read_paper), and examine the methodology sections in detail via the source manuscripts (mcp__arxiv-latex__get_paper_abstract, get_paper_prompt, list_paper_sections, get_paper_section).
5. Store key findings in the knowledge graph (memory) so they can be referenced later.
6. Create a Word document Literature_Review.docx in the workspace containing: an introduction (overview of RAG and why it matters for knowledge-intensive NLP), one dedicated section per paper (title, authors, year, main contribution, methodology discussion), and a conclusion (synthesize themes, common patterns, future research directions). It must read as a flowing academic literature review.

IMPORTANT EXECUTION CONSTRAINTS TO ACCOUNT FOR IN THE PLAN:
- Literature_Review.docx must be created EXACTLY ONCE by exactly one designated agent, only after ALL paper content is gathered. Agents researching subsets of papers must NOT create/write/overwrite/append Literature_Review.docx; they must return findings in reports or write to their own separately named intermediate files.
- Parallelizable work should be identified: e.g., researching each of the 5 papers can be done in parallel by separate agents (each writing its own intermediate findings file, e.g. findings_paper_N.md), with one designated agent assembling the final document.
- The plan must specify, for each subtask: dispatch decision (self / explore / coder), and whether it is independent (parallelizable) or must wait for another subtask's output.

DELIVERABLE: Return an ordered list of subtasks, each with: a short title, dispatch decision, dependencies (which subtask it waits on), and a 1-3 sentence description of what it does and its acceptance criteria. Keep it concise and actionable.

   - mcp__arxiv-latex__get_paper_prompt (arxiv_id=<PAPER_ID>) if you need the precise LaTeX formulation of the method (equations, notation).
4. Judge relevance once more on full read: if the paper is genuinely about RAG, proceed. (It is expected to be; if you find it is NOT about RAG, say so prominently at the top of your findings file.)
5. WRITE YOUR FINDINGS FILE. Create exactly one file: <FINDINGS_FILE> in the workspace root (/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/<FINDINGS_FILE>) using mcp__filesystem__write_file. Do not write anything else.

CONTENT REQUIREMENTS for the findings file (markdown):
- Paper title, FULL author list, publication year, venue (e.g., NeurIPS/ICLR/arXiv preprint).
- The angle this paper covers (original RAG formulation / survey / self-reflective retrieval / recursive retrieval / practical system building).
- Main contribution: 2-4 sentences.
- Detailed methodology discussion: architecture, training procedure, retrieval mechanism/index, key design choices, evaluation setup and headline results (include concrete numbers/benchmarks where the paper states them).
- How the paper relates to the thesis threads above (retrieval design & factual accuracy, retrieval granularity, evaluation).
- Everything must be grounded in the actual paper content you read. DO NOT fabricate details, numbers, or claims.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: <FINDINGS_FILE> exists in the workspace root, is complete markdown, has accurate bibliographic metadata, and contains a substantive methodology analysis with concrete details from the actual paper. Report back a short summary (title, year, venue, one-line contribution, and the path of your findings file).

You are the SOLE designated assembler for a PhD thesis literature review document. Your job is to create the Word document `Literature_Review.docx` EXACTLY ONCE, in the workspace root, using the Word MCP tools. No other agent creates, writes, or modifies this file — it is exclusively yours. Do NOT create any other files.

WORKSPACE ROOT (use absolute paths):
/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace

CONTEXT: A PhD student is writing Chapter 2 (literature review) on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Their thesis tracks: (1) how retrieval design improves factual accuracy and context relevance, (2) the relationship between retrieval granularity (sentence/paragraph/document/summary level) and generation quality, (3) evaluation of RAG systems (attribution quality, retrieval relevance, faithfulness). Five papers were researched in depth, and each has a complete findings file that you MUST read before writing:

- /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/findings_paper_1.md  → Lewis et al. 2020, "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" (NeurIPS 2020) — ORIGINAL RAG FORMULATION
- /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/findings_paper_2.md  → Gao et al. 2023, "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey" — SURVEY
- /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/findings_paper_3.md  → Asai et al. 2024, "Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection" (ICLR 2024) — SELF-REFLECTIVE RETRIEVAL
- /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/findings_paper_4.md  → Sarthi et al. 2023/2024, "RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval" (ICLR 2024) — RECURSIVE RETRIEVAL
- /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/findings_paper_5.md  → Chen et al. 2024, "From RAG to Rich: Building Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems" — PRACTICAL SYSTEM BUILDING

STEP 1 — Read all five findings files with mcp__filesystem__read_text_file. They contain everything you need (bibliographic metadata, main contribution, detailed methodology, results, relation to thesis).

STEP 2 — Create the document. Use the Word MCP tools (mcp__word__*):
1. mcp__word__create_document with filename="/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_deepseek-v4-flash/SingleUserTurn-academic-literature-review/workspace/Literature_Review.docx" and title "Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Literature Review" (author optional).
2. Build the document with mcp__word__add_heading (levels 1 and 2) and mcp__word__add_paragraph. Structure and content requirements:

**Title page / heading**: "Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Literature Review" (Heading 1). Optionally a subtitle line "Chapter 2 — Literature Review" as a paragraph.
